questions.q: You tap "Transfer ₦5,000 to Tunde" in a banking app. Where does the backend fit in?
questions.explain: The phone only sends a request and shows the answer. The backend, on another computer, checks who you are and whether you have the money, updates both accounts, saves the change, and replies. The screen you tap is the front end.
options: It is the screen of the app where you tapped the button
It is a program on another computer that checks the request, moves the money, saves the change and answers the app
It is the part of the phone that stores your account balance
It is the app store the banking app was downloaded from

questions.q: In a to-do app, which part is the front end?
questions.explain: The front end is the part you see and touch. The tasks themselves live on another computer, where the backend stores them and answers the app's requests.
options: The screen that shows your tasks and the buttons you tap
The program that stores the tasks on another computer
The database where the tasks are written down
The framework the backend is built with

questions.q: ZudoJS is a framework. What does that mean?
questions.explain: A framework gives you ready-made parts so you do not write everything from zero. ZudoJS is written in TypeScript and gives you parts for backends. The program that runs JavaScript on a server is Node.js.
options: A set of ready-made, tested parts for building backends
A programming language that replaces JavaScript
A program that runs JavaScript on a server
A code editor that looks like Visual Studio Code

questions.q: Why does the academy teach HTTP, databases, security and even your own mini framework before ZudoJS?
questions.explain: ZudoJS is the destination, not the starting point. After building the pieces by hand, the framework is no longer magic: you understand the problem each part solves.
options: Because ZudoJS is only unlocked after you finish every other lesson
So that when you meet ZudoJS you know what each part does for you, and can fix it when something goes wrong
Because frameworks are rarely used in real jobs
Because ZudoJS cannot be used without writing a framework first

questions.q: How is the academy organised, from biggest to smallest?
questions.explain: Six tracks group 19 levels. Each level is a course, a course is split into modules, and a module into lessons. Tiers are labels on courses and lessons, not a level of the structure.
options: Tracks, then levels (each one a course), then modules, then lessons
Lessons, then modules, then courses, then tracks
Parts, then chapters, then pages
Tiers, then tracks, then lessons, then modules

questions.q: In which order do the six tracks come?
questions.explain: Each track builds on the ones before it: reasoning, then the language, then types, then backend engineering without a framework, then ZudoJS, then production.
options: Thinking, JavaScript, TypeScript, Backend engineering, ZudoJS, Production
JavaScript, Thinking, TypeScript, ZudoJS, Backend engineering, Production
Thinking, TypeScript, JavaScript, Backend engineering, Production, ZudoJS
ZudoJS, Backend engineering, TypeScript, JavaScript, Thinking, Production

questions.q: What is level 1 about?
questions.explain: Level 1 is the Thinking track. You learn to reason about a problem before you write serious code.
options: Installing Node.js and writing a web server
Programming thinking: breaking problems down, algorithms, pseudocode, logic and a little mathematics
The ZudoJS command-line tool
TypeScript's type system

questions.q: There are 19 levels but 20 courses. Why?
questions.explain: Every level is a course, except level 4, which has two courses at the same level. So 19 levels hold 20 courses.
options: One course is a practice course with no lessons
The capstone counts twice
Level 4 has two courses side by side: Advanced JavaScript, and JavaScript in the browser and on the server
The Welcome lesson is a course of its own

questions.q: Which levels form the ZudoJS track?
questions.explain: Levels 12 to 15 are ZudoJS: fundamentals, application development, advanced systems and architecture. Levels 7 to 11 are Backend engineering, and 16 to 19 are Production.
options: 1 to 4
7 to 11

questions.q: What is special about the Backend engineering track (levels 7 to 11)?
questions.explain: The Backend engineering track works with no framework, so you see every problem a framework solves before you meet ZudoJS in level 12.
options: It is taught only with ZudoJS
It teaches HTTP, databases, APIs, security and architecture without a framework
It is optional for everyone
It only covers front-end development

questions.q: How is the Task API built during the academy?
questions.explain: You write the Task API by hand with Node.js at level 4. From level 12 you rebuild it with ZudoJS, add a database, users, permissions, events, background jobs and tests, and later deploy and monitor it.
options: Only once, with ZudoJS from the start
First by hand with plain Node.js, then rebuilt with ZudoJS and grown with a database, users, events and more
In Python first, then in JavaScript
Only in the browser terminal, never on your computer

questions.q: The BookStore API is written in TypeScript with no framework. What is that for?
questions.explain: Building a real backend by hand, with PostgreSQL, authentication and tests, shows you the repeated work a framework removes. The capstones are ShopFlow and the SaaS platform, not the BookStore API.
options: ZudoJS cannot be used for shops
TypeScript projects are not allowed to use frameworks
It shows you the problems a framework exists to solve
It is the final capstone of the academy

questions.q: Why do you build your own mini framework at level 11?
questions.explain: Once you have written a small container, router, middleware and validation yourself, you can read any framework, ZudoJS included, and understand what it does.
options: To replace ZudoJS in the later levels
So no framework is magic: you have built a container, a router, middleware and validation yourself
Because the capstone must use your own framework
To publish it instead of learning TypeScript

questions.q: Which two capstones end the academy at level 19?
questions.explain: ShopFlow is a complete commerce backend. The SaaS platform is a production-grade system that many customer companies share safely. A capstone is a final project that uses everything you learned.
options: The Task API and the BookStore API
ShopFlow and a SaaS platform
Your mini framework and the Task API
A calculator and a guessing game

questions.q: Which of these does a course page NOT show?
questions.explain: A course page shows the level, track, tier, time, prerequisites, your progress, the outcomes, the project, the modules and the checkpoint. There are no accounts, so there are no other learners' scores to show.
options: What you will be able to do when you finish, and what you build
The modules with their lessons in order
A course checkpoint
Other learners' scores

questions.q: How does the course checkpoint work?
questions.explain: The checkpoint draws 20 questions from all the lesson tests of the course. Get 16 right to pass. Five questions with 4 to pass is the lesson test.
options: 5 questions from one lesson; 4 to pass
20 questions picked at random from the tests of every lesson in the course; 16 to pass
One long project that a teacher marks
50 questions; every answer must be right

questions.q: You fail a lesson test with 3 of 5. What happens next?
questions.explain: The test picks five questions at random from a bank of 30 to 50. A retry gives you five different ones, so you cannot pass by remembering answers: you have to understand the lesson.
options: The lesson is locked for a day
You must restart the whole course
You read the explanations, look at the lesson again, and take a new test with five different questions
The same five questions come back until you pass

questions.q: A lesson header says LEVEL 5 · LESSON 3 OF 23. What does it tell you?
questions.explain: The header gives the level of the course the lesson belongs to, and where the lesson sits in that course. Level 5 is the TypeScript course.
options: You have finished 5 levels and 3 lessons
The lesson is the 3rd of 23 in the level 5 course
The lesson takes 5 minutes and has 3 examples
You scored 3 out of 23 in the test

questions.q: What is the By the end of this lesson you can box for?
questions.explain: The objectives say what you will be able to do after the lesson. Read them first, and at the end ask yourself honestly whether you can do each one.
options: It lists the lessons you must finish first
It lists what the lesson teaches, so you can check yourself against it at the end
It shows your test results
It lists the files the editor will create

questions.q: What is the best way to use a Reason it out box?
questions.explain: The value is in doing the thinking before you see the code. Comparing your own answer with the worked reasoning shows you what you missed.
options: Open Show the reasoning straight away to save time
Skip it: it has no code, so it is not important
Answer its questions yourself first (what you know, what can go wrong, the edge cases), then compare with the reasoning
Copy its questions into the editor and run them

questions.q: An example is marked Node.js only. Why can it not run in the browser?
questions.explain: Browsers may not read your files or start servers. Examples that do must run on your own computer with Node.js.
options: Because it contains a mistake
It uses things a browser is not allowed to do, like reading your files or starting a web server
Because it prints more than two lines
Because the browser terminal only runs TypeScript

questions.q: A box shows $ node --version. What do you type in your terminal?
questions.explain: A line starting with $ is a command, but you do not type the $ itself. The lines under it are what the computer printed back.
options: $ node --version
node --version
$node--version
v24.19.0

questions.q: Where is your progress (finished lessons, test results, checkpoints) saved?
questions.explain: There is no account and nothing is sent anywhere. Your progress lives in the browser you use.
options: In your account on the academy's server
In a file in your projects folder
In this browser, on this device only
It is not saved at all

questions.q: You did ten lessons on your laptop. Tonight you open the academy on your phone. What do you see?
questions.explain: Progress is saved in one browser on one device. Another browser or device starts fresh. Clearing the browser's site data also removes it.
options: Your ten lessons, because they are synced to your account
A fresh start: progress saved in the laptop's browser is not on the phone
Only the lessons you passed with 5 of 5
An error asking you to log in

questions.q: How does the Continue where you left off button know where you stopped?
questions.explain: The progress bars and the Continue button read what this browser has saved: which lessons you finished and which one you opened last.
options: It asks the academy's server
It reads the progress saved in your browser
It always goes to lesson 1
It guesses from the time of day

questions.q: A course is labelled Foundation. What does that tell you?
questions.explain: Foundation means it is needed before you continue, like Programming thinking, JavaScript fundamentals and TypeScript.
options: Learn it when your application needs it
Learn it when you prepare an application for deployment
You must understand it before moving on
It is for experts only

questions.q: ZudoJS advanced systems is an Advanced course. What does that mean for you?
questions.explain: Advanced means "learn it when your application needs it". It is not forbidden, just not required before you move on.
options: You must finish it before any other course
Learn it when your application needs it
Beginners are not allowed to open it
It is required for every ZudoJS project

questions.q: Sam has never written code. Where should Sam start?
questions.explain: Complete beginners follow every level. Each new word is explained the first time it appears, so skipping means missing those explanations.
options: At ZudoJS fundamentals, because that is the goal
At TypeScript, to skip JavaScript
At the next lesson, Your developer environment, and then every level in order
At the capstone, to see the end result first

questions.q: Chidi writes Python at work and has never used JavaScript. Where should Chidi start?
questions.explain: Chidi already thinks like a programmer, so level 1 can be skipped. The language is what is new, so he starts at /learn/javascript.
options: At JavaScript fundamentals (level 2)
At ZudoJS fundamentals (level 12)
At TypeScript (level 5)
At Production engineering (level 17)

questions.q: Kemi builds websites with JavaScript and has never used types. Where should Kemi start?
questions.explain: People who know JavaScript start at /learn/typescript. ZudoJS assumes types, HTTP, databases and security, which Kemi has not learned yet, so jumping to level 12 would leave big gaps.
options: At level 1, with no skipping
At TypeScript (level 5)
At ZudoJS fundamentals (level 12)
At the capstone (level 19)

questions.q: Lee builds TypeScript backends every day. Where should Lee start?
questions.explain: TypeScript backend developers go straight to /learn/zudo-fundamentals. When a lesson uses something they skipped, it links back to the lesson that teaches it.
options: At Your developer environment
At JavaScript fundamentals
At TypeScript
At ZudoJS fundamentals, following links back when something is new

questions.q: You think you already know the material of a course. What is a quick, honest way to check before you skip it?
questions.explain: The checkpoint draws questions from every lesson of the course, so it tests exactly what the course teaches. Missed questions point to the lessons you need.
options: Read only the course title
Take the course checkpoint: if you pass, move on; if not, the missed questions show which lessons to read
Mark every lesson as done
Skip it, and come back only if the capstone fails

console.log("Tracks:", 6, "Levels:", 19);

Hello! I am learning backend engineering.
Tracks: 6 Levels: 19
Hello! I am learning backend engineering. Tracks: 6 Levels: 19

"Hello! I am learning backend engineering."
"Tracks:", 6, "Levels:", 19

Hello! I am learning backend engineering.
Tracks:6Levels:19

questions.explain: A program runs from top to bottom. Each console.log prints its own line, in the order the lines are written.
options:
Thinking
JavaScript
TypeScript

TypeScript
JavaScript
Thinking
Thinking JavaScript TypeScript

questions.explain: The quotes only mark where the text starts and ends. console.log prints the text inside them.
questions.code: console.log("I want to build an API.");
options: I want to build an API.
"I want to build an API."
console.log("I want to build an API.")

questions.explain: The commas in the code separate four values. console.log prints them with one space between each, and the commas themselves are not printed.
options: ZudoJS: levels 12 to 15
ZudoJS: levels12to15
ZudoJS: levels, 12, to, 15
ZudoJS: levels 12, to 15

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first line prints the number 19, the second the text "19". On their own they look the same: console.log does not show a text's quotes.

questions.q: What does this print?

options:
Task API

TaskAPI

questions.q: Course pages live under /learn/. What does this print?
questions.explain: + between two texts glues them together exactly, with nothing added or removed.
options: /learn/typescript
/learn/ typescript
"/learn/" + "typescript"
/learn//typescript

options: Tracks after TypeScript: 3
Tracks after TypeScript: 6 - 3
Tracks after TypeScript: 63

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Text is printed exactly as written, capital letters included. The computer does not "fix" your spelling.

questions.q: A checkpoint has 20 questions. What does this print?
questions.explain: Two console.log calls give two lines. 20 - 16 has no quotes, so it is calculated: 4 wrong answers still pass.
options:
Pass mark: 16 of 20
Allowed mistakes: 4

Pass mark: 16 of 20
Allowed mistakes: 20 - 16
Pass mark: 16 of 20 Allowed mistakes: 4

Pass mark:16of20
Allowed mistakes:4

questions.q: Write one line of code that prints exactly Hello, ZudoJS Academy!
questions.explain: Put the text in quotes inside console.log( ). It prints the text without the quotes.

questions.q: Print the six tracks, one per line, in order: Thinking, JavaScript, TypeScript, Backend engineering, ZudoJS, Production.
questions.explain: Six console.log calls give six lines, top to bottom, in the order the tracks build on each other.
questions.starter: // print the six tracks, one per line
questions.expected:
Thinking
JavaScript
TypeScript
Backend engineering
ZudoJS
Production

questions.q: This program prints the Task API's journey in the wrong order. Fix it so it prints Plain Node.js, then ZudoJS, then Deployed, one per line.
questions.explain: Lines run from top to bottom, so the order of the lines is the order of the output. The Task API is written by hand first, rebuilt with ZudoJS, and finally deployed.

questions.q: Use one console.log with two values (a text and a number) to print Start at level: 5
questions.explain: Separate the two values with a comma: console.log("Start at level:", 5);. console.log adds one space between them.

questions.q: Use + to join "/learn/" and "zudo-fundamentals", and print the result: /learn/zudo-fundamentals
questions.explain: + between two texts joins them exactly, so you get the address of the ZudoJS fundamentals course.
questions.starter: // join the two texts with + and print the result

questions.q: Print the two capstones on one line, with a single console.log and two values: ShopFlow SaaS platform
questions.explain: Two values separated by a comma are printed with one space between them. You could also write "ShopFlow " + "SaaS platform", but then you must add the space yourself.
questions.starter: // one console.log, two values: "ShopFlow" and "SaaS platform"
